questions.title: RA variant — exception
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a recognised variant of rheumatoid arthritis?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a true variant, so not the answer). Felty syndrome is a recognised RA variant, combining splenomegaly, pancytopenia, lymphadenopathy and vasculitis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a true variant, so not the answer). Caplan syndrome is a recognised RA variant, combining pneumoconiosis with rheumatoid arthritis.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a true variant, so not the answer). The juvenile forms (oligoarticular, polyarticular, Still's disease) are recognised RA variants defined by age of onset.
explanations.D: Correct. Rheumatoid arthritis has no congenital variant — it is an acquired, inflammatory autoimmune disease, not a condition present from birth. "Congenital rheumatoid arthritis" is not a recognised entity, unlike Felty syndrome, Caplan syndrome and the juvenile-onset forms.

questions.learning_objective: Identify which item in a listed set of conditions is not a true variant of rheumatoid arthritis.

field_notes.keySource: source B recall fragment: "Non of RA variants -> congenital"

questions.author_notes: Source B carries only a bare topic+answer fragment (no option text); this stem and its distractors (the three genuine RA variants) were authored by this lane from standard teaching, corroborated by src_a51388c9442af6f01df5 p.15's own named-variants list.

questions.title: Most common form of arthritis
questions.question: Which of the following is the most common form of arthritis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Rheumatoid arthritis is common but affects a smaller proportion of the population than osteoarthritis overall.
explanations.B: Correct. Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis, a degenerative rather than inflammatory joint disease that becomes increasingly prevalent with age, particularly from about 45 years and usually over 60. This makes it the arthritis most students and clinicians encounter overall, even though it is not the most inflammatory or the most feared.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gout is a common crystal arthropathy but is considerably less prevalent overall than osteoarthritis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ankylosing spondylitis is a comparatively uncommon condition (roughly 0.2% prevalence), far less common than osteoarthritis.

questions.learning_objective: State that osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis.

field_notes.keySource: source B recall fragment: "Most common form of arthritis -> osteoarthritis"

questions.title: Septic arthritis — not part of management
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the standard management of septic arthritis?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS part of management, so not the answer). Joint drainage/aspiration is a core part of septic arthritis management, removing purulent material and relieving pressure.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS part of management, so not the answer). Systemic antibiotics targeting the causative organism are essential septic arthritis treatment.
explanations.C: Correct. Blood transfusion has no role in treating septic arthritis itself — it is not part of standard management of the joint infection and would only be given for a separate, unrelated indication if one existed. Confusing a serious hospital intervention with a genuine treatment step is the trap this question is built around.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this IS part of management, so not the answer). Analgesia is a routine supportive component of septic arthritis management.

questions.learning_objective: Identify blood transfusion as NOT part of standard septic-arthritis management.

field_notes.keySource: source B recall fragment: "Not of septic arthritis management -> blood of transfusion"

questions.author_notes: Source B carries only a bare topic+answer fragment; this stem and its distractors (the genuine management steps) were authored by this lane from standard teaching.

questions.title: Scleroderma — not a feature
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature or association of scleroderma (systemic sclerosis)?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a feature, so not the answer). Raynaud's phenomenon is a common and characteristic feature of scleroderma.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a feature, so not the answer). Oesophageal dysmotility is a recognised gastrointestinal feature of scleroderma.
explanations.C: Correct. Reiter's disease (reactive arthritis) is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy — associated with preceding Chlamydia trachomatis or enteric infection, asymmetric oligoarthritis, conjunctivitis and mucocutaneous lesions — and is not a feature or association of scleroderma, which is a separate connective-tissue disease with its own distinct manifestations. The two conditions are managed and classified under entirely separate disease families despite both appearing in the same rheumatology curriculum.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this IS a feature, so not the answer). Skin fibrosis and calcinosis are core features of scleroderma, including the CREST syndrome variant.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise Reiter's syndrome as belonging to the seronegative-arthritis family, not to scleroderma.

field_notes.keySource: source B recall fragment: "Not of scleroderma -> reiter's disease"

questions.title: CREST syndrome — ten-year survival
questions.question: A patient with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome) asks about her long-term outlook. What is the approximate ten-year survival for this form of the disease?

explanations.A: Incorrect. This substantially underestimates the survival taught for limited scleroderma/CREST.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This underestimates the survival taught for limited scleroderma/CREST.
explanations.C: Correct. Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (CREST syndrome) carries roughly 70% ten-year survival, a substantially better prognosis than diffuse systemic sclerosis, because its skin-and-peripheral-vessel-predominant disease specifically spares the severe early internal-organ involvement of diffuse disease. This is notably better than the outlook for diffuse systemic sclerosis, which involves earlier, more severe internal-organ disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This overestimates the survival figure taught for limited scleroderma/CREST.

questions.learning_objective: State that limited scleroderma/CREST carries roughly 70% ten-year survival.

field_notes.keySource: source B recall fragment: "CREST prognosis -> 70% survival at 10 years" (same fact as source A's A20)

questions.title: Raynaud's phenomenon — drug to avoid
questions.question: A patient with Raynaud's phenomenon needs treatment for coexisting hypertension. Which class of antihypertensive drug should be avoided?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this is NOT the drug to avoid). Calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine are vasodilators and are actually the treatment of choice for Raynaud's phenomenon, not a drug to avoid.
explanations.B: Correct. Beta-blockers are avoided in Raynaud's phenomenon because their vasoconstrictor effect can precipitate or worsen digital vasospastic attacks, unlike most other antihypertensive classes, which do not share this specific counterproductive action. Vasodilators such as calcium channel blockers are used instead when an antihypertensive is needed in this context.
explanations.C: Incorrect. ACE inhibitors are not specifically contraindicated in Raynaud's phenomenon and do not share beta-blockers' vasoconstrictor liability.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Angiotensin receptor blockers are not specifically contraindicated in Raynaud's phenomenon and do not share beta-blockers' vasoconstrictor liability.

questions.learning_objective: Identify beta-blockers as the drug class to avoid in a patient with Raynaud's phenomenon.

field_notes.keySource: source B recall fragment: "Avoid -> beta blocker" (Raynaud's phenomenon context)

questions.author_notes: Source B carries only a bare topic+answer fragment; this stem and its distractors were authored by this lane from standard teaching, corroborated by src_a51388c9442af6f01df5 p.21's Raynaud's treatment section (vasodilators favoured).

questions.title: Morning back pain — ankylosing spondylitis
questions.question: A young man reports chronic low back pain that is worst on waking and improves within the first hour of getting up and moving. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. Morning back pain that improves with activity is the classic inflammatory back pain pattern of ankylosing spondylitis, typically presenting in young men and often accompanied by a positive family history and HLA-B27 association. The direction of the movement-response — better with activity — is the key discriminator from a mechanical cause.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lumbar disc prolapse classically causes pain worsened by movement/straining and often radicular leg symptoms, not a pattern that improves with morning activity.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mechanical low back pain characteristically worsens with activity and improves with rest — the opposite pattern to this case.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vertebral compression fracture typically presents with acute, activity-related pain (often in an older or osteoporotic patient), not a chronic activity-improved pattern in a young man.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise ankylosing spondylitis from activity-improved morning back pain in a young man.

questions.title: Gout — thiazide and purine-rich diet case
questions.question: A man taking a thiazide diuretic and with a diet high in meat and seafood presents with sudden severe pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. This vignette combines the classic risk factors for acute gout — a thiazide diuretic (which reduces renal urate excretion) and a high dietary purine intake (meat, seafood) — with the classic presentation of podagra, acute pain and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Both risk factors act through the same underlying mechanism, raising serum urate until it crystallises in the joint.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reactive arthritis typically follows a genitourinary or gastrointestinal infection and involves an asymmetric large-joint oligoarthritis, not this specific risk-factor and joint pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Septic arthritis is a differential that must be excluded by joint aspiration, but this vignette's specific risk-factor combination (thiazide, high purine diet) points more directly to gout.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pseudogout more typically affects the knee, wrist or hip in an older patient and is not classically linked to thiazide use or dietary purine intake in the way gout is.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise acute gout from a case combining thiazide use, a high-purine diet and podagra.

field_notes.keySource: source B recall fragment: "Male, thiazide, high meat/purine intake -> acute gout arthritis" (duplicate of A06)

questions.title: Gout — supportive investigation (recall)
questions.question: For the patient above with suspected acute gout, which readily available blood test would best support the diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. Serum uric acid is raised in most gout patients and is the standard supportive laboratory investigation, even though joint aspiration with polarized-light microscopy remains the gold-standard confirmatory test. It is used alongside the clinical picture, even though joint aspiration with crystal microscopy remains the gold-standard confirmatory test.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Serum calcium is not the relevant supportive test for gout; abnormal calcium metabolism is more relevant to pseudogout risk factors (e.g. hyperparathyroidism).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Rheumatoid factor is relevant to rheumatoid arthritis serology, not to gout, a crystal arthropathy unrelated to autoantibody status.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ANA is relevant to connective tissue disease serology (e.g. SLE), not to gout.

questions.learning_objective: Name serum uric acid as the standard supportive investigation for gout.

questions.title: Gout management — withdrawal of thiazide
questions.question: For the same patient once the acute gout attack is treated, what change to his existing drug therapy is most appropriate?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Allopurinol is chronic urate-lowering therapy, but it is deliberately delayed until several weeks after the attack has settled, not started immediately.
explanations.B: Correct. General management of gout removes the precipitating cause — in this case, the thiazide diuretic, which raises serum urate by reducing its renal excretion. Withdrawing it (and substituting an alternative antihypertensive if needed) is the specific, appropriate step for a patient whose gout is linked to this known drug trigger.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Loop diuretics can also raise urate and are not a safe substitute chosen specifically to help this patient's gout.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Continuing the precipitating drug unchanged would leave the patient at ongoing risk of further gout attacks.

questions.learning_objective: Identify withdrawal of the precipitating drug (a thiazide diuretic) as the appropriate management step after a gout attack linked to it.

field_notes.keySource: source B recall fragment: "Gout management -> Withdrawal of thiazide" (duplicate of A08)

questions.title: Seronegative arthritis — defining serology
questions.question: The seronegative arthritides (ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthropathy, IBD-associated arthritis) are characterised by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A positive rheumatoid factor is the defining serology of rheumatoid arthritis, the seropositive counterpart this group is contrasted against.
explanations.B: Correct. The seronegative spondyloarthropathies — ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthropathy and IBD-associated arthritis — are, by definition, rheumatoid-factor negative, distinguishing them serologically from rheumatoid arthritis. They instead share a strong HLA-B27 association.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Anti-CCP antibody positivity is specific to rheumatoid arthritis, not to the seronegative arthritides.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ANA positivity is more relevant to connective tissue diseases such as SLE, not to the seronegative spondyloarthropathies as a defining feature.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a negative rheumatoid factor as the defining serology of the seronegative spondyloarthropathies.

field_notes.keySource: source B recall fragment: "seronegative arthritis characterized -> -ve rheumatoid factor"
